title: Vernon Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Vernon wells have a 270-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $15,400-$26,800.
h1: What Vernon, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Vernon means treating the well as part of the property, not a minor utility detail. Records within 5 miles show 431 permitted wells, including 158 recorded as constructed. Of the wells reporting depth, the median is 270 feet, and the middle half runs from 202 to 330 feet.

Production looks stronger than in many uncertain rural-well areas: the reported yield median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with 67% of reported wells at 15 gallons per minute or more. That still does not guarantee what a new hole will produce. Permit records, neighboring wells, aquifer information, and a proper site evaluation should all be part of your decision.

sections.heading: Vernon well depths and the plains geology
sections.html:
Vernon wells are commonly deeper than a shallow domestic well. Among 236 records reporting total depth, the median is 270 feet. The middle half falls between 202 and 330 feet, the 90th percentile is 376 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 438 feet.

The depth mix helps a driller price the job: 58% are between 100 and 300 feet, while 39% are between 300 and 600 feet. Only 4% are under 100 feet, and none are reported at 600 feet or more. Permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 304 wells, the Ogallala for 126, and the High Plains Aquifer for 4. Those differences can matter from one lot to the next, so a bid should allow for local conditions rather than assume the median is a guarantee.

sections.heading: How much water Vernon wells produce
sections.html:
Yield records are available for 98 wells. Their median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 11.0 and 25.0 gallons per minute. Two-thirds of those reported wells, or 67%, produce 15 gallons per minute or more. Another 33% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported well in this set is under 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for a household buyer, but it is not a promise for an unbuilt well. Yield depends on the formation, completion, pump setting, and testing method. Ask for the actual well construction and pump-test documents, not just a seller’s statement that the well has “good water.” DWR permit records can show what was authorized and reported, but they do not replace a current inspection.

sections.heading: Vernon water levels and the measurement trend
sections.html:
Only 23 wells report a static water level, so this part of the record is thinner than the depth data. The median depth to water is 155 feet, with the middle half between 130 and 180 feet below the surface. That gives a useful planning range for pump and electrical discussions, but it is not a site-specific water level.

The decade medians move from 142 feet below surface in the 1960s to 175 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water was measured deeper in the more recent records, but the small number of reported measurements and differences in locations and conditions make it unsafe to call this a confirmed regional decline. A buyer should obtain the well’s own static level and recent pumping information before sizing equipment.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Vernon, and when
sections.html:
Vernon’s permit history is long but uneven. The records include 6 permits from the 1950s, 16 from the 1960s, 43 from the 1970s, 25 from the 1980s, 42 from the 1990s, 28 from the 2000s, 26 from the 2010s, and 14 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Use mix includes domestic or household wells at 35%, stock at 29%, irrigation at 48%, and monitoring at 1%.

The most active names in these records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc. with 48 permits, Schaal Drilling Co. with 14, and Zion Drilling Service with 11. Those counts describe recorded activity, not current availability or a recommendation. For a new project, verify licensing, references, access requirements, casing and grout specifications, and the proposed completion plan.

sections.heading: What a new Vernon well may cost
sections.html:
For Vernon’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35-$55 per foot. At the 270-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $9,400-$14,800. This is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $15,400-$26,800 at that median depth. A lot with difficult access, extra casing, deeper-than-expected drilling, or unusual electrical and trenching needs can fall outside that range. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the driller must continue past the planned depth. Compare the completion details, not just the per-foot rate.

sections.heading: Vernon risks to check before closing
sections.html:
Low yield is not the leading signal in the reported sample, but the sample includes only 98 yield records. Dry-hole risk and water-quality risk still need a property-specific review. The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 54 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. There are 0 historic mine features in that mapped area. These mapped sites do not prove a problem at a particular address, but they are a reason to test rather than assume.

Check the well permit, construction report, casing and grout, pump test, static water level, and laboratory results. Confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, and the proposed house location before drilling. A Colorado DWR permit controls what the well may legally serve. In over-appropriated basins, an augmentation plan may be needed, and an exempt household-use well still has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Vernon, Wray, and Yuma
sections.html:
Before buying a lot, map the nearest permitted wells and separate domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring records. Vernon’s records include wells tied to the Ogallala and High Plains Aquifer as well as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer descriptions, so nearby wells are useful evidence but not a substitute for a site investigation. Review properties around Wray, Laird, Eckley, Idalia, Yuma, and Kirk only as local comparisons; the well at your address remains the important one.

For a build, make the well location, septic field, reserve area, driveway, and utility trench part of one site plan. Budget using the $15,400-$26,800 finished-well model, then keep room for a deeper hole or added site work. If the property already has a well, make the purchase contingent on records, inspection, water testing, and a satisfactory flow test.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Vernon, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Vernon is 270 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 202 to 330 feet, while the 90th percentile is 376 feet and the deepest record is 438 feet. Most wells are between 100 and 300 feet, but 39% are between 300 and 600 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Vernon, Colorado?
faq.a: The drilling model for Vernon uses $35-$55 per foot in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 270-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,400-$14,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,400-$26,800.

faq.q: How much water do Vernon wells produce?
faq.a: Among 98 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 11.0-25.0 gallons per minute. The records show 67% producing 15 gallons per minute or more, while 33% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Individual results can differ.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Vernon, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular Vernon well is safe to drink. About 10 miles of the area contains 54 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, review construction records, and retest after any treatment or well work.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Vernon, Colorado?
faq.a: The limited reported measurements show a median static water level of 142 feet below surface in the 1960s and 175 feet in the 2020s. Only 23 wells report static water levels, so this suggests deeper recent measurements but does not confirm a regional decline. Get the specific well’s current static level and pumping information.
